input: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first. That is the recommendation under consideration, and the other plants are held until results from Plant 2 are reported. The firm runs 3 plants and revenue is $82 million per year, so the delivery problem is not a marginal one for a business of this size. The evidence base is the order records for 12 months, covering 11777 orders, and those records show on-time delivery over the last two quarters at 89%, against a target of 95%. Late delivery is concentrated rather than evenly spread: Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders. Overtime cost was $1.8 million last year, up 23% on the year before, and the order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 1.5 weeks a year ago, which suggests that the present way of working is absorbing pressure through overtime rather than clearing it. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $286k; Plant 2 alone is $151k. An internal estimate, which is not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. The pattern matters for the choice being considered. Because the late orders sit mainly at one plant, a system installed everywhere at once would spend the full quoted amount before any site had shown whether the overtime saving is real. A staged start limits the initial commitment to the plant where the problem is largest, and it gives the operations director a reported result, drawn from the firm's own orders, on which the later decision can rest. The operations director owns the scheduling programme, and the decision is whether to accept the staged route, with Plant 2 as the test case, before committing the remaining plants.

The larger extension is considered only after the reported saving at Plant 2 is known, and the remaining plants enter the programme on the strength of a measured result rather than on the strength of the estimate alone.
